title: The trial
hook: he was flogged for refusing a state doctrine that the Qur'an was created

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Musnad, and your line: a vast collection. What did someone tell you, and did you write down who told it? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-six.

A room in the caliph's palace, and a man in chains. The question put to him is short: is the Qur'an created? Say yes, and you go home. Judges have said yes. Other scholars, under pressure, have said yes. He won't. He asks his questioners for a verse of the Qur'an, or a word from the Prophet, that says it. They don't give him one he accepts. So the whips come out. The man is Ahmad ibn Hanbal, the collector from yesterday, and the ordeal has a name.
screen: `A MAN IN CHAINS, ONE QUESTION.` → `SAY YES, AND GO HOME.` → `HE WON'T.`

segments.voice: The name is the mihnah: the trial, the ordeal. It began under the caliph al-Ma'mun. His court had taken up a position held by a group of theologians called the Mu'tazila: that the Qur'an, as God's speech, was created, not eternal with God. They held it, as they understood it, to protect God's oneness. If the Qur'an is eternal alongside God, they asked, aren't there two eternal things? Ahmad and the hadith scholars around him held the opposite: the Qur'an is the speech of God, and God's speech is not a created thing. The caliph ordered judges and scholars to be questioned on it. One after another, people gave way. Ahmad refused. He was imprisoned, and under the next caliph, al-Mu'tasim, he was flogged. The reports keep returning to one reply of his during the questioning: give me something from the Book of God or the sunnah of His Messenger, and I'll say it. Look at what he was and wasn't doing. He wasn't trying to win a philosophy debate on the court's terms. He was refusing to make the texts say something he didn't find in them. In the end he was released, and later, under another caliph, the mihnah was brought to an end. The Qur'an speaks about testing too. God will try people, it says, with something of fear and hunger, and loss of wealth and lives and crops, and it gives good news to those who are patient. To be fair to both sides: the Mu'tazila saw themselves as defending God's unity, and Ahmad saw himself as defending the text. Muslim theologians still study both arguments. What the story keeps, especially in the Hanbali school, is the picture of one scholar who would not say it.
screen: `MIHNAH: THE TRIAL.` · `WAS THE QUR'AN CREATED?` · `GIVE ME A VERSE, AND I'LL SAY IT.` · `FAIR TO BOTH SIDES.`

segments.voice: The practice: stand firm on one conviction. Choose one thing you live by. Not an opinion you'd argue online. Something you actually keep: you don't lie to your kids, you keep the fast, you show up when you said you would. Name it in one plain sentence. Then picture the pressure that might bend it: a tired evening, a boss, a friend's teasing. Breathe, and say the sentence again, quietly. You don't need to fight anyone. Just know where you stand. If you pray, you can ask to be kept firm. The bell holds the time.
Mihnah. Trial, ordeal: the caliph's test that demanded scholars say the Qur'an was created, and that Ahmad ibn Hanbal refused. Today's word.
Your line: he would not say it. Today, if you're about to say something you don't mean just to keep things smooth, try a quiet, honest answer instead. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Hanbali scholars and students tell the story of Ahmad ibn Hanbal's trial as an example of steadfastness, and Sunni creeds state that the Qur'an is the uncreated speech of God.

original.note: Arabic: trial, ordeal; the name for the caliphs' test of scholars over whether the Qur'an was created.

trapdoor: what you thought: a trial means a court case.
what it means: the mihnah, a test the caliph's court put to scholars over whether the Qur'an was created.
what a scholar hears: khalq al-Qur'an, the Mu'tazili argument from God's oneness, and Ahmad's demand for a text.

notes: Mu'tazili position (Qur'an created) and their reasoning from God's oneness: confirm the summary is fair to them.
'Many gave way' (judges and scholars who affirmed under pressure): confirm framing; it describes those questioned, not Muslims at large.
Imprisonment, flogging under al-Mu'tasim, later release, and the end of the mihnah under a later caliph (al-Mutawakkil): confirm. Dates and the number of lashes left out under the claims rule.
Ahmad's repeated reply ('give me something from the Book of God or the sunnah of His Messenger'): confirm as reported.
howItsDone says Sunni creeds 'commonly' state the Qur'an is uncreated speech; confirm wording (Ash'ari and Maturidi formulations differ in detail).
